summary: This informational document discusses using an Autonomic Control Plane to give network operations a stable connection to devices. Operations tools usually rely on the network being managed, which creates circular dependencies, especially when bringing up devices. An autonomic control plane can avoid that.

plainLanguage.summary: If you fix the radio using only the radio, you are stuck. This gives network fixers a second, always-working road to reach broken devices.

subtitle: A separate IPv6 network inside your switches for management, immune to routing changes.

tldr.problem: Network Operations and Management (OAM) relies on connectivity provided by the network being managed, creating a circular dependency. Provisioning new devices requires OAM to already work. Changing routing or addressing can break OAM connectivity. Historically, providers used separate physical networks (Data Communications Networks) for OAM, but cost is prohibitive for most organizations.
tldr.mechanism: An Autonomic Control Plane (ACP) is a separate in-band IPv6 network built automatically inside network devices using mutual authentication and encryption. It operates independently of the data plane routing. OAM tools connect via the ACP, which remains stable even during data-plane changes, bootstrap failures, or network reconfigurations.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes practical deployment options ranging from simple (OAM tools connecting via ACP IPv6 addresses) to long-term (autonomic NMS hosts fully participating in the ACP, with dual connectivity and path-selection policies). It addresses challenges like IPv4-only NOC legacy systems, path selection, and security.

today: RFC 8368 is an Informational document published in May 2018. It describes architectural use cases and deployment strategies for in-band OAM planes. The IETF ANIMA working group continues to evolve the Autonomic Control Plane (ACP) specification. The guidance in this RFC remains current for organizations designing OAM strategies for large networks.

sections.title: The Circular Dependency Problem
sections.content:
Operational tasks depend on network connectivity provided by the network being managed. Bootstrapping new devices requires connecting to them, which requires connectivity that does not yet exist. Making large routing or addressing changes (like switching from IPv4 to IPv6, or merging networks) cannot be automated because OAM cannot afford to lose connectivity during the transition.

This forces sequential, manual "expanding ring" configuration from a Network Operations Center, with tight dependencies between provisioning and OAM tool operations. It makes automation fragile and complex.

Historically, large service providers built separate Data Communications Networks (DCNs)—entirely separate IP networks carrying only OAM traffic—to avoid this problem. But building and operating a separate network is too expensive for smaller providers, enterprises, and IoT deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: You cannot fix the network using the network if the network is broken. A separate OAM network lets you fix it anyway.

sections.title: Generalized Autonomic Control Plane (GACP)
sections.content:
The RFC defines an in-band OAM network called the Generalized Autonomic Control Plane (GACP). It has several key properties: VRF isolation (separate routing and forwarding from the data plane), IPv6-only addressing using Unique Local Addresses (ULAs) that auto-address without external allocation, mutual authentication and encryption between GACP devices using cryptographic credentials, and a clear boundary (only explicitly configured traffic is allowed in and out).

The GACP must be "autonomic"—its operation cannot be disrupted by NMS or SDN configuration affecting the data plane. Data-plane changes affect only the data plane; the GACP is unaffected.

Because the GACP uses ULAs (which do not route globally and require local DNS), it is inherently isolated and secure against external injection. GACP extends through the network and can provide access to NOC (Network Operations Center) equipment either directly or via edge devices.
sections.plainLanguage: The ACP is a private IPv6 network inside each switch. They find each other automatically, encrypt everything, and keep working no matter what happens to the regular network.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC describes several practical approaches to deploying an ACP for OAM.

Simplest: ACP edge devices connect to NOC via a subnet and leak the GACP natively to NMS hosts as IPv6 connectivity. Hosts use SSH, SNMP, and NETCONF over the GACP. This requires only IPv6 support in NMS hosts.

Intermediate: NOC hosts support both GACP and data-plane connectivity simultaneously, preferring the data plane for performance but falling back to GACP on failure. This is tricky in IPv4-only environments and requires NAT translation or dual-stack support.

Long-term: NMS hosts themselves become autonomic and join the GACP, eliminating the need for special edge devices or translation. This is simpler and more secure in the long run but requires development work on NMS products.
sections.plainLanguage: You can start simple: NOC talks to the ACP, which talks to the devices. Later, the NOC itself joins the ACP. Eventually, everything is on the ACP and much simpler.

sections.title: Handling IPv4-Only NOC Systems
sections.content:
Many NOC backend systems do not yet support IPv6, creating a challenge because GACP is IPv6-only. The RFC describes stateless IP/ICMP translation (SIIT) with Explicit Address Mapping (EAM), which translates between GACP IPv6 addresses and IPv4 addresses allocated to NOC systems. This creates a 1:1 mapping: each NOC host or GACP device has a corresponding address in the other address family.

This is a short-term workaround. The long-term goal is for all NOC systems to support IPv6 natively. NAT64 and other translation mechanisms can also work but are less flexible. The key insight is that translation should happen at GACP edge devices to maintain security isolation.
sections.plainLanguage: If the NOC only speaks IPv4, a translator between the ACP and the NOC can convert addresses back and forth. Not ideal, but it works until the NOC is upgraded.

sections.title: Path Selection and Dual Connectivity
sections.content:
The GACP is not expected to have high performance because security and reliability are the priorities, not throughput. For tasks where data-plane connectivity is available and stable, using the data plane is preferable for performance. For operations that would break the data plane (like major routing changes), the GACP should be used exclusively.

Ideal policies require the NOC host transport stack to support fallback: try to build a data-plane flow, but if it fails, fall back to GACP. Multipath TCP (MPTCP) and Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) can support part of this. The RFC also suggests using DNS names to steer traffic (name.noc.example.com for data plane only, name-acp.noc.example.com for GACP only).

For software downloads and other high-volume tasks, traffic policing at the GACP edge protects the GACP from overload.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the fast highway when it is working, but always be ready to use the slow but reliable ACP path if the highway breaks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The GACP provides mutual authentication and encryption using cryptographic credentials shared by devices in the same GACP domain. ULAs ensure that GACP traffic does not leak into the global Internet and is naturally filtered. Device certificates derive both the GACP address and cryptographic identity from a trusted bootstrap process (BRSKI).

When OAM tools connect via the GACP, they can use TLS/DTLS with GACP credentials for end-to-end encryption. If data-plane connectivity is also used (for performance), it should also be encrypted using the same GACP credentials to maintain security expectations.

Operator misconfiguration or bugs could still cause GACP leakage during mergers, acquisitions, or network reconfigurations. Physical security of NOC links connecting to GACP edge devices is essential. If reverse DNS is set up for GACP ULAs (which is optional), it should be managed automatically from the device certificate infrastructure to ensure consistency.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything on the ACP is encrypted and signed with certificates so only trusted devices join. It is isolated from the Internet. The weak point is the physical cable from the NOC to the ACP edge, which must be physically locked.
